$comment: The central conceptual diagram of the transit work: why A* cannot do transit, and what RAPTOR does instead.

meta.title: Why Transit Needs a Different Algorithm - A* vs RAPTOR

image_prompt: Create an educational comparison poster, flat modern style, 16:9, split into a LEFT half and a RIGHT half by a vertical divider. LEFT HALF titled 'Driving - time-INDEPENDENT': a small road graph with a path from A to B and edge labels showing distances in km, plus a caption 'the road is 2.1 km long at 6am and at 6pm - the answer does not depend on when you ask'. Add a small clock icon crossed out. RIGHT HALF titled 'Transit - time-DEPENDENT': draw a TIMETABLE-style diagram instead of a road graph - a horizontal time axis running 17:40 to 18:20, with three horizontal lanes labelled 'walk', 'Bus 8', 'walk'. Show a walking bar from 17:42 to 17:46, then a WAITING gap shaded grey from 17:46 to 17:48 labelled 'you must be there BEFORE the bus leaves', then a solid orange ride bar from 17:48 to 18:05, then a final walking bar 18:05 to 18:09. Add a prominent clock icon and the caption 'miss the 17:48 and the entire rest of the plan changes'. ACROSS THE BOTTOM, a full-width strip titled 'RAPTOR - rounds are transfers' with four numbered circles left to right: 'Round 0: everywhere you can WALK to', 'Round 1: everywhere reachable after ONE boarding', 'Round 2: after one transfer', 'Round 3: after two transfers', each with a small widening map blob beneath it showing the reachable area growing. Caption the strip: 'each round adds one more vehicle, so the first time a stop is reached is also the fewest-transfers way to reach it'.

style.look: educational diagram, flat modern, generous whitespace, teaching-poster clarity
principles: Show the mechanism, not just the name. A reader should finish understanding WHY it works.
Prefer one worked example with real numbers over an abstract restatement.
Use colour to encode state (frontier / visited / chosen), never for decoration.
Keep formulas large and readable; put them in their own panel, not inside a node.

spec.the_core_insight: A* searches a graph whose edge weights never change. Transit edges only exist at specific moments - you cannot 'traverse' the 17:48 bus at 17:52. That makes it a time-dependent shortest-path problem, which is a different class of algorithm.

comparison.transit: a specific vehicle departing at a specific minute

comparison.aspect: Does the answer depend on when you ask?

comparison.transit: arrival time AND number of transfers, together
a first-class cost - standing at a stop is part of the trip
RAPTOR - Round-bAsed Public Transit Optimized Router

raptor.key_idea: Work in rounds, where round k = the best you can do using at most k vehicles. No priority queue and no heuristic - just repeated sweeps over the routes touching the stops you have already reached.

rounds.means: every stop you can reach on foot from the origin
everywhere reachable after boarding exactly one vehicle

raptor.why_it_is_fast: Each round is a linear scan over the routes that touch newly improved stops, with no heap operations at all. It is cache-friendly and needs no preprocessing, which is why it is the standard choice for schedule data that changes every few weeks.
raptor.bonus: Because round k means 'at most k vehicles', RAPTOR naturally produces the whole Pareto set - fastest trip, fewest-transfers trip, and the useful compromises in between - in one pass.

spec.who_runs_it: OpenTripPlanner 2.9, not our own code. Hand-rolling RAPTOR plus the walk-to-stop stitching, calendar exceptions, and realtime updates is a project in itself; OTP already does it correctly.
annotations: This is the single most important idea in the transit work. Everything else - the container, the graph build, the GraphQL proxy - exists because of it.
Other algorithms in this family: Connection Scan (CSA), which sweeps timetable connections in departure order, and time-dependent Dijkstra, which is the simplest and the slowest.
